paragraphs: Aeschylus was born around 525 BCE near Athens and fought as a hoplite at the Battle of Marathon, an experience his epitaph, by his own reported wish, mentioned before any of his plays. He is credited with adding a second actor to tragic performances, which turned recited narration into dialogue and, with it, into drama capable of conflict onstage.

Of roughly eighty plays he is thought to have written, seven survive complete, including the Oresteia, the only full trilogy to come down from Greek tragedy. Ancient sources report he died in Sicily after a tortoise, dropped by an eagle mistaking his bald head for a rock, struck and killed him, a story too neat to trust but repeated for over two thousand years.

Akhenaten was born Amenhotep, a younger son of Amenhotep III who was not raised to expect the throne. Some scholars think his elder brother Thutmose, who died young, was meant to rule instead, which would make Akhenaten's accession around 1353 BCE something closer to an accident of succession than a planned reign.

Once crowned, he closed temples to Egypt's other gods, elevated the sun disc Aten above them, and moved the capital to a new city, Akhetaten, built on empty desert land specifically because it belonged to no other god. The move was reversed within a generation of his death, and his name was chiselled from monuments so thoroughly that later king lists skip straight over him.

Archimedes was born around 287 BCE in Syracuse, on Sicily, and studied for a time in Alexandria before returning home to work under the patronage of the city's king. Most of what is known about his life comes from later biographers, especially Plutarch, writing well over a century after his death.

He calculated a close approximation of pi, worked out the mathematics behind levers and buoyancy, and designed war machines that, according to Roman accounts, helped Syracuse hold off a siege for two years. He was killed in 212 BCE when the city finally fell, reportedly by a Roman soldier he had ignored while absorbed in a geometry problem drawn in sand.

Aristophanes was born around 446 BCE and began staging comedies in Athens while barely out of his teens, a fact he later joked about in prologues addressed directly to the audience. Eleven of his roughly forty plays survive, the only complete examples of Old Comedy to come down from antiquity at all.

Lysistrata, in which Athenian and Spartan women withhold sex to force an end to war, was staged in 411 BCE, during a real and increasingly desperate phase of the Peloponnesian War. His comedies mocked living politicians and philosophers by name onstage, including Socrates in The Clouds, a satire performed while its target was still walking the streets of Athens.

Aristotle was born in 384 BCE in Stagira, in northern Greece, the son of a physician at the Macedonian court, a connection that later put him in position to tutor the young Alexander the Great around 343 BCE. He studied at Plato's Academy for two decades before leaving, reportedly passed over for its leadership after Plato's death.

His surviving works, many likely lecture notes rather than polished treatises, cover logic, biology, ethics, politics and physics, and shaped European university curricula so thoroughly that medieval scholars simply called him the Philosopher, no name required. Much of his biology, based on direct dissection, held up better under later scrutiny than his physics did.

Ashoka was born around 304 BCE into the Mauryan royal family and came to the throne after a succession struggle that, by some later Buddhist accounts, involved killing rival brothers, though the details vary between sources written centuries afterward. His early reign as emperor continued the aggressive expansion his grandfather Chandragupta had begun.

That changed with the conquest of Kalinga around 261 BCE, a war so costly that Ashoka's own rock edicts, inscriptions he had carved across the subcontinent, describe his remorse and his subsequent turn to Buddhist principles of non-violence. Those edicts, written in vernacular languages rather than the usual courtly Sanskrit, are also some of the earliest surviving Indian texts addressed directly to ordinary subjects.

Attila was born around 406 CE somewhere in the Hunnic territories north of the Danube; no Roman or Hunnic source records the place, and most of what is known about his early life comes from Roman diplomats who dealt with him as an adult rather than any account of his childhood. He ruled jointly with his brother Bleda from 434 CE until having him killed around 445 CE.

Roman writers who met him in person, notably the envoy Priscus, described a court of considerable wealth surrounding a leader who dressed plainly and ate from wooden plates while his officers used gold and silver. Attila's raids reached deep into both the Eastern and Western empires before he died in 453 CE, reportedly of a nosebleed on his wedding night, and his empire fragmented among his sons within a year.

Constantine was born in 272 CE in Naissus, in the Balkans, to Constantius, a Roman military officer who would later become emperor, and Helena, a woman of low social status whom Constantius set aside for a more advantageous marriage. Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his father's troops in 306 CE and then spent nearly two decades fighting rivals to make that claim real across the whole empire.

In 313 CE he issued the Edict of Milan with his co-emperor Licinius, ending state persecution of Christians and returning confiscated property to the church, though he did not make Christianity the empire's official religion himself. In 330 CE he dedicated a new capital on the site of the old Greek city of Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople after himself.

Cyrus was born around 600 BCE, the son of a Persian vassal king under the Median empire; the famous legend that his grandfather Astyages ordered him killed as an infant, only for a herdsman to raise him instead, comes from Herodotus writing over a century later and reads more like a folk tale pattern than history.

What is documented independently is his conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE and the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay foundation text in which he presents himself as a liberator of the city's gods and people rather than a destroyer. It has since been read, sometimes overread, as an early statement on religious tolerance, though it was also standard Mesopotamian propaganda for a new king.

Darius was born around 550 BCE to a noble Achaemenid family, not the direct royal line, and took the Persian throne in 522 BCE by killing a man he claimed was an imposter occupying it. The Behistun Inscription, a monumental relief he had carved into a cliff face, tells this version of events in three languages, in Darius's own words, which makes it useful history and unreliable evidence at once.

Once in power he reorganised the empire into provinces called satrapies, standardised coinage and taxation, and began building Persepolis as a ceremonial capital. The palace complex, excavated from the nineteenth century onward, still shows the reliefs of tribute-bearers from across the empire that Darius commissioned to advertise its reach.

Diogenes was born around 412 BCE in Sinope, on the Black Sea coast, and arrived in Athens, by most accounts, after being exiled from his home city over a coin-debasing scandal involving his father's mint. Poverty in Athens became the philosophy itself rather than an accident of it.

Ancient biographers say he lived in a large ceramic storage jar rather than a house, walked the streets in daylight carrying a lamp claiming to search for an honest man, and once, told by Plato that a plucked chicken fit Plato's own definition of a featherless biped, brought one into the Academy's lecture hall. Most of this comes from Diogenes Laertius, writing centuries later, and the stories were likely already sharpened into legend by then.

Epicurus was born on the island of Samos in 341 BCE to Athenian parents settled there as colonists, and he studied philosophy under teachers linked to Democritus's atomist tradition before founding his own school in Athens around 306 BCE. He called it the Garden, and unusually for the time it admitted women and enslaved people as members alongside free men.

His idea of pleasure as life's aim is often misremembered as indulgence, but his own writings recommend simple food, steady friendships and freedom from fear of death and the gods, arguing that the wildest excesses cause more pain than they relieve. Only fragments and a few complete letters of his vast output survive, mostly preserved by later followers rather than in his own manuscripts.

Almost nothing is recorded about Euclid's life beyond that he taught in Alexandria around 300 BCE, probably during the reign of Ptolemy I; even his birthplace is unknown, and later ancient biographies confuse him at points with the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara.

What survives instead is the Elements, thirteen books building geometry up from a small set of definitions and postulates, a structure so influential that it stayed a standard textbook, with only minor revision, into the twentieth century. Abraham Lincoln reportedly studied it by candlelight to sharpen his legal reasoning, a detail that says more about the book's reach than anything known about the man who wrote it.

Euripides was born around 480 BCE, by tradition on the day of the Battle of Salamis, though ancient biographers liked tidy coincidences and this one may simply be too convenient to trust. He wrote roughly ninety plays across a long career, of which nineteen survive, more than any other Greek tragedian, largely by chance of manuscript survival rather than ancient acclaim.

His Athenian audiences found him unsettling: he gave female and enslaved characters extended reasoning voices, questioned the gods' justice openly, and was mocked by Aristophanes for it in comedy performed in his own lifetime. He left Athens near the end of his life for the Macedonian court, where he died, reportedly, before finishing his final play.

Hadrian was born in 76 CE, likely in Rome to a family from Italica in Spain, and was raised partly under the guardianship of his relative Trajan after his father's early death. He served under Trajan on campaign and was, by disputed accounts, adopted as heir only on Trajan's deathbed in 117 CE, a succession clean enough to invite suspicion that it was arranged after the fact.

Where Trajan had expanded the empire, Hadrian spent much of his reign consolidating it, touring the provinces in person and ordering the construction of a stone and turf wall across northern Britain, begun around 122 CE, to mark and defend a fixed frontier rather than push further north. Substantial stretches of that wall still stand.

Hannibal was born in Carthage in 247 BCE to Hamilcar Barca, a general who, according to the historian Livy, made his young son swear an oath of eternal enmity toward Rome before an altar. Whether the oath is fact or later legend, Hannibal spent his career fighting the war it describes.

In 218 BCE he led an army, including a small number of war elephants, across the Alps into Italy, a crossing so costly in men and animals that only a fraction of the elephants survived it. He won major battles at Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, yet Rome refused to surrender, and Hannibal spent fifteen years campaigning on Italian soil without ever capturing the city itself.

No inscription records the day Hatshepsut was born, only the reign into which she was born, around 1507 BCE, as a daughter of Thutmose I. What survives instead is the record she built later: statues, temple reliefs and inscriptions at Deir el-Bahari recut, decades after her death, to show a king rather than a queen who ruled as one.

Her throne name, Maatkare, appears on obelisks and on trade expedition texts describing voyages to Punt for incense and ivory. Officials writing about her sometimes used male grammatical forms, sometimes female, an inconsistency historians now read less as confusion than as evidence of a court working out how to describe a woman holding a role every text assumed was male.

Herodotus was born around 484 BCE in Halicarnassus, a Greek city then under Persian control, which may explain why he wrote about the Persian side with more curiosity than contempt. He travelled widely across Egypt, Persia and the Black Sea coast, describing customs, geography and monuments he claimed to have seen firsthand.

Cicero later called him the father of history, but the title came with a rival nickname too: Aristotle and others accused him of being the father of lies, for reporting griffins guarding gold and men with dogs' heads alongside sober military detail. Modern archaeology has since confirmed enough of his geography and customs to rehabilitate much, though not all, of his reputation.

No fact about Homer's birth is secure enough to state as fact. Ancient sources disagree on his home city, name a dozen candidates from Smyrna to Chios, and disagree on his era by centuries; Herodotus put him around 850 BCE, others earlier. The date used here, around 800 BCE, is a convention, not a record.

What survives is the poetry, transmitted orally for generations before being fixed in writing, and a scholarly argument that has run since the eighteenth century over whether one person composed the Iliad and the Odyssey at all, or whether Homer is the name later editors gave to a tradition of many poets. The uncertainty is itself the oldest fact about him.

Lao Tzu is traditionally dated to 601 BCE and traditionally identified as a court archivist named Li Er, but the earliest sources that mention him, Sima Qian's history written some four centuries later, already admit uncertainty about whether he was one man or several. No contemporary record of his life exists at all.

The Tao Te Ching itself, the text his name is attached to, likely accreted from multiple contributors over generations rather than arriving from a single hand. Archaeologists found versions of it buried in tombs at Mawangdui and Guodian, centuries apart and differing in wording, which is roughly the closest thing to physical evidence the tradition has.

Marcus Aurelius was born in Rome in 121 CE to a senatorial family, and was singled out for imperial succession as a child by the emperor Hadrian, who arranged for his own successor Antoninus Pius to adopt the boy as heir. He spent decades being groomed for a throne he would not actually hold until 161 CE.

Much of his reign was spent commanding troops on the frontier against Germanic tribes rather than governing from Rome, and the Meditations, the private notebook he is remembered for, was written during those campaigns as personal Stoic exercises never intended for publication. It survived by chance transmission and became one of the most widely read texts of Stoic philosophy only long after his death.

Nefertiti's birth, around 1370 BCE, left no record of her parentage; she may have been Egyptian nobility or, by one theory, a Mitanni princess sent to seal an alliance. What is certain is that she married Akhenaten and appears beside him in more temple reliefs than any queen before her, driving a chariot and making offerings to the Aten in scenes usually reserved for kings.

The painted limestone bust that made her famous was found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Akhetaten, one plaster-coated practice piece among many, never intended for display. It sat in a German museum for over a decade before its 1924 unveiling turned an unfinished study into the most reproduced face of ancient Egypt.

Nero was born in 37 CE at Antium, to Agrippina the Younger, whose marriage to the emperor Claudius and relentless manoeuvring got her son adopted ahead of Claudius's own biological son Britannicus. Agrippina is widely suspected, though not proven, of poisoning Claudius in 54 CE to put fifteen-year-old Nero on the throne while she still controlled him.

He later had his own mother killed once she became inconvenient, and Roman writers, largely hostile senators writing after his fall, blamed him for singing while Rome burned in 64 CE and for using Christians as scapegoats for the fire, a detail Tacitus records independently of Nero's own later reputation for cruelty. He died by his own hand in 68 CE as army revolts closed in, ending the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

Ovid was born in 43 BCE in Sulmo, east of Rome, to a family that expected him to pursue law and public office, a path he tried and abandoned in favour of poetry. His early work was frankly erotic, and it made him famous in Rome well before he turned to the mythological retellings that would outlast the scandal.

The Metamorphoses, completed around 8 CE, strings together some 250 myths of transformation into a single continuous narrative, from the creation of the world to Julius Caesar becoming a star. That same year Augustus exiled Ovid to a remote outpost on the Black Sea, for reasons never stated plainly in surviving sources, and he died there roughly a decade later, still writing but never recalled.

Plato was born in Athens around 428 BCE to an aristocratic family with connections on both sides to earlier Athenian statesmen. He first trained for a political career, but the trial and execution of his teacher Socrates in 399 BCE, on charges of corrupting the young, turned him against Athenian democracy as it then operated and toward philosophy instead.

He founded the Academy around 387 BCE on land just outside Athens, an institution that ran for centuries after his death and is sometimes called the first university in the Western tradition. Nearly all his surviving work takes the form of dialogues rather than treatises, most of them starring Socrates, which leaves scholars still arguing over where the teacher's ideas end and the student's begin.

Almost nothing survives about Ptolemy's personal life beyond that he worked in Alexandria around 100 to 170 CE, using observational records kept there and in Babylon going back centuries before his own time. Even his first name and family background are unrecorded; he is known only by the name attached to his books.

His Almagest set out a mathematical model of a stationary Earth with the sun, moon and planets circling it on nested spheres, detailed enough to predict eclipses and planetary positions with real accuracy. That geocentric model went essentially unchallenged in both the Islamic and European scholarly worlds for roughly fourteen centuries, until Copernicus and later Kepler replaced it.

Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos around 570 BCE and later settled in Croton, in southern Italy, where he founded a community that mixed mathematics with strict dietary rules, secrecy oaths and a belief in the transmigration of souls. He wrote nothing down himself; everything attributed to him comes from followers writing after his death.

The theorem bearing his name was already known, in specific numerical cases, to Babylonian and Egyptian mathematicians centuries earlier. What the Pythagorean school likely contributed was a general proof and, more lastingly, the idea that number itself explained the structure of the physical world, an idea that outlasted every detail of his biography.

Ramesses was born around 1303 BCE to a father, Seti I, who was not himself born to rule. His grandfather Ramesses I had been a military commander elevated to found a new dynasty, so the boy was raised from early childhood as a designated heir, given military commands and his own household years before he took the throne around age twenty-five.

His reign, which ran some sixty-six years, is documented less by any single record than by sheer volume: temples at Abu Simbel and Karnak, a peace treaty with the Hittites preserved in both Egyptian and Akkadian copies, and a mummy so recognisable that when it flew to Paris in 1976 for fungal treatment, Egypt issued it a passport listing its occupation as king, deceased.

Sappho was born on Lesbos around 630 BCE into a family wealthy enough that her exile at one point, ordered for unclear political reasons, took her to Sicily rather than anywhere harsher. Almost none of this comes from Sappho herself; it is pieced together from later biographers writing centuries after she died.

Of the roughly nine books of verse ancient scholars attributed to her, only one poem survives complete, quoted whole by a later critic illustrating a point about style. The rest exists as fragments, some recovered from papyrus used to stuff mummified crocodiles in Roman Egypt, scraps that still shape how the word lyric is understood.

Seneca was born around 4 BCE in Corduba, in Roman Spain, to a wealthy family of Roman citizens, and was sent to Rome as a child for the education expected of a future senator. He built a career as advocate, essayist and playwright before Emperor Claudius exiled him to Corsica in 41 CE on charges linked to a court affair.

Recalled to tutor the young Nero, he became the emperor's chief adviser for the early, relatively stable years of the reign, then watched that same emperor turn on him. Nero eventually forced Seneca to take his own life in 65 CE on suspicion of conspiracy, a death Tacitus describes at length as calm and deliberately staged to match the Stoic philosophy Seneca had spent his career writing about.

Solon was born in Athens around 630 BCE to a family of modest noble standing; ancient biographers say he took up trade as a young man partly because his father had given away much of the family's wealth. That mercantile background, unusual for an Athenian lawgiver, put him in contact with ordinary debtors and creditors before he ever held office.

Appointed archon around 594 BCE amid a crisis of debt bondage, he cancelled outstanding debts secured on people's bodies, opened political offices beyond the old aristocracy, and then, according to Plutarch, left Athens for ten years so nobody could pressure him into amending the laws himself.

Sophocles was born around 497 BCE in Colonus, near Athens, to a family wealthy enough from arms manufacturing that he received a full education in music and athletics before ever writing a play. He first defeated the established Aeschylus in the Athenian dramatic competition in 468 BCE, a result ancient sources say the judges reached only after the city's leading general was drafted in to break a tie.

He is credited with introducing a third actor into tragedy, which let him build scenes of direct confrontation, such as Antigone's clash with Creon, that two speakers could not sustain. Of some 120 plays attributed to him, only seven survive whole, and he was reportedly an Athenian general and a treasury official alongside a writing career that outlasted several wars.

Sun Tzu is traditionally placed in the sixth century BCE as a general serving the state of Wu, but the text bearing his name, The Art of War, contains passages some scholars date to the later Warring States period, generations after he supposedly lived. Whether one general wrote it or it accumulated over time is unresolved.

A 1972 excavation at Yinqueshan uncovered bamboo strips confirming the text existed by the second century BCE, along with a related but distinct work attributed to a descendant, Sun Bin. The find settled the book's antiquity without settling anything about the man; its advice to win without fighting has been read by strategists from feudal Japan to modern business schools.

Thucydides was born in Athens around 460 BCE to a family with property near Thrace, wealth that let him serve as an elected general in the Peloponnesian War before the war itself derailed his career. In 424 BCE he was blamed for the loss of Amphipolis to a Spartan force and exiled from Athens, a punishment that gave him two decades to write rather than fight.

His history of that war deliberately excludes the gods as causes, sources speeches through reconstruction rather than invention, and states outright that he checked competing eyewitness accounts against each other. The method, more than any single fact he recorded, is why historians still cite him as the discipline's first methodological break from Herodotus.

Trajan was born in 53 CE in Italica, in southern Spain, one of the first Roman emperors to come from a family settled outside Italy itself. He rose through a conventional military career under the Flavian emperors before Nerva, needing to shore up support from the army, adopted him as heir and successor in 97 CE.

Under Trajan the empire reached its largest territorial extent, following conquests in Dacia and a campaign against Parthia in the east. He also funded large public building programmes, including a new forum and market complex in Rome and a harbour at Ostia, projects the Senate later cited when granting him the honorific title optimus princeps, the best ruler.

Virgil was born near Mantua in 70 BCE to a family of modest landowning stock, and his early poetry, the Eclogues and Georgics, dealt with farming and rural life partly because his own family's land had been threatened by confiscations during the civil wars that followed Julius Caesar's assassination.

He spent the last decade of his life writing the Aeneid at the emperor Augustus's encouragement, tracing Rome's founding back to a Trojan refugee, and died in 19 BCE before finishing it to his own satisfaction. He reportedly asked for the manuscript to be burned unpublished; Augustus overruled him, and the unfinished epic became the standard school text of the Roman world instead.

Cicero was killed on 7 December 43 BCE, hunted down while fleeing after Mark Antony placed his name on the proscription lists drawn up by the Second Triumvirate. Ancient sources say he leaned his head out of the litter carrying him and offered his throat to the soldiers rather than resist further.

On Antony's specific order his hands, the hands that had written the Philippics attacking him, were cut off along with his head and nailed up on the Rostra in the Roman Forum, the platform Cicero had once used to address the Senate. Cassius Dio adds that Antony's wife Fulvia took the severed head onto her lap and pierced the tongue with a hairpin.

Leonidas died holding the pass at Thermopylae in 480 BCE after a local shepherd, Ephialtes, showed Persian forces a mountain track that let them encircle the defenders. Herodotus records that Leonidas sent most of his allied troops away once the position was lost and stayed with a much smaller core, roughly the three hundred Spartans plus other holdouts, to fight to the end.

The Persians beheaded his body and displayed the head on a stake, an act Herodotus presents as unusual cruelty by Xerxes' own standards. Decades later the Spartans recovered his remains and reburied him at home, and the site still carries an inscribed epitaph honouring those who obeyed the order to stand and not retreat.

Spartacus, a Thracian gladiator, led an escape from a training school at Capua in 73 BCE that grew into an army of escaped slaves numbering in the tens of thousands. Rome sent successive commanders against him before finally committing Marcus Licinius Crassus with a force large enough to end the revolt in 71 BCE.

According to the historian Appian, Spartacus was wounded in the thigh in the final battle, sank to one knee behind his shield, and was killed along with most of his remaining fighters; his body was never identified afterward. Six thousand of his surviving followers were crucified along the Appian Way, a line of crosses stretching for miles as a deliberate warning to travellers.

Xerxes was murdered in his own bedchamber in 465 BCE, not on any battlefield he had commanded personally. The killer was Artabanus, the commander of his royal bodyguard, who according to ancient accounts acted with a eunuch's help and then briefly tried to seize power himself by pinning the murder on Xerxes' son Darius.

The plot unravelled within months; another son, who took the throne as Artaxerxes I, had Artabanus killed once the truth came out. It was an unglamorous end for a king remembered abroad chiefly for the failed invasion of Greece a decade and a half earlier, and Persian court sources on his final years are thin compared with the Greek accounts of Thermopylae and Salamis.
